question: What is the main difference between an impairment and a disability?

options.A: An impairment only affects children, while a disability only affects older adults.
options.B: An impairment is a bodily difference, while a disability is often created by environmental barriers.
options.C: An impairment is temporary, whereas a disability is always permanent.
options.D: A disability is purely psychological, while an impairment is strictly physical.

explanation: Impairment refers to the actual structure or function of the body, but the physical and social environment often turns that impairment into a functional disability. [learn more](GNS225_U5_T9#GNS225_U5_T9_h1)

question: Why must nurses shift their focus from curing to optimizing health when caring for patients with permanent physical disabilities?

options.A: Because chronic conditions rarely respond to any nursing interventions at all
options.B: Because hospital policies prohibit long-term treatment plans for chronic illnesses
options.C: Because patients prefer to manage their own healthcare without professional assistance
options.D: Because many physical impairments are irreversible, making functional independence the primary goal

explanation: When an impairment cannot be reversed, nursing care prioritizes maximizing independence, comfort, and quality of life instead of a cure. [learn more](GNS225_U5_T9#GNS225_U5_T9_h1)

question: Which body areas require the closest inspection during a routine skin assessment for an immobile patient?

options.B: The palms of the hands and soles of feet
options.C: Soft fatty areas of the upper abdomen
options.D: Exposed areas on the face and neck

explanation: Prolonged pressure over bony prominences reduces blood supply, making these areas the primary sites for pressure injuries in immobile patients. [learn more](GNS225_U5_T9#GNS225_U5_T9_h2)

question: A nurse is assessing a patient who uses a wheelchair full-time. Which oversight represents a common mistake in clinical practice?

options.A: Failing to check routine preventative screenings like blood pressure and dental health
options.B: Asking the patient about their daily routine for bathing and dressing
options.C: Evaluating the patient for chronic muscle spasms and nerve pain
options.D: Inspecting the skin over the sacrum and heels for early redness

explanation: Clinicians often fixate on the visible disability and neglect general preventative healthcare that all patients require. [learn more](GNS225_U5_T9#GNS225_U5_T9_h2)

question: What is the primary purpose of involving physical therapists in the care of a patient with a mobility impairment?

options.A: To design safe mobility plans and select appropriate assistive devices
options.B: To cook specialized nutritional meals for rehabilitation
options.C: To perform daily hygiene and bathing tasks for the patient
options.D: To prescribe routine medications for chronic neuropathic pain

explanation: Physical therapists specialize in restoring and maintaining movement, making them vital partners in choosing mobility aids and creating exercise regimens. [learn more](GNS225_U5_T9#GNS225_U5_T9_h3)

question: Why should a nurse avoid rushing a patient during a bed-to-wheelchair transfer?

options.A: Rushing damages the mechanical lift machine's motor.
options.B: Rushing instantly drains the patient's long-term energy stores.
options.C: Rushing causes patient anxiety and increases the risk of a fall.

explanation: Taking time during transfers ensures proper body positioning, reduces fear, and keeps both nurse and patient stable. [learn more](GNS225_U5_T9#GNS225_U5_T9_h3)

question: How often should a bedbound patient be turned to help prevent pressure injuries?
explanation: Turning a bedbound patient at least every two hours relieves pressure on bony prominences and restores blood flow to vulnerable tissues. [learn more](GNS225_U5_T9#GNS225_U5_T9_h4)

question: What is the primary cause of joint contractures in a person with severe physical immobility?

options.A: Sudden increases in blood pressure during physical exertion
options.B: Bacterial infections traveling from the bladder into the joint space
options.C: Permanent shortening of muscles and tendons from lack of movement
options.D: Excessive intake of dietary calcium forming deposits in the joints

explanation: When joints remain in one position without movement, the surrounding soft tissues shorten and stiffen, resulting in a contracture. [learn more](GNS225_U5_T9#GNS225_U5_T9_h4)

question: Which simple home modification helps prevent dangerous tripping hazards for someone using a walker?

options.A: Removing loose throw rugs from the floors
options.B: Adding decorative floor mats near doorways
options.C: Waxing hardwood floors until they shine
options.D: Placing heavy wooden furniture in hallways

explanation: Loose throw rugs easily bunch up under mobility aids like walkers and wheel tips, creating a major fall hazard. [learn more](GNS225_U5_T9#GNS225_U5_T9_h5)

question: Why are grab bars installed in bathrooms for individuals with physical disabilities?

options.A: To block water from splashing onto the bathroom floor tiles
options.B: To hold towels and washcloths within easy reach of the bathing area
options.C: To serve as hanging storage for lightweight assistive devices
options.D: To provide stable support during transfers on and off the toilet or in the shower

explanation: Wet bathroom surfaces combined with transfers make grab bars essential safety features for preventing falls. [learn more](GNS225_U5_T9#GNS225_U5_T9_h5)

question: What is a common emotional response experienced by a person who has recently acquired a permanent physical disability?

options.A: Complete indifference toward their physical health status
options.B: Immediate and permanent acceptance of the new lifestyle
options.C: Euphoria over lifestyle changes and reduced responsibilities
options.D: Grief and a process similar to mourning a loss

explanation: Patients frequently experience a grief reaction as they process the loss of their previous physical abilities and independence. [learn more](GNS225_U5_T9#GNS225_U5_T9_h6)

question: Why is respite care an important recommendation for family members caring for a person with a physical disability?

options.A: It permanently relieves family members of all financial responsibilities.
options.B: It teaches family members advanced physical therapy techniques.
options.C: It provides the patient with professional psychological counseling.
options.D: It gives exhausted family caregivers temporary relief to prevent burnout.

explanation: Respite care offers temporary relief for caregivers, protecting their physical and mental well-being against severe burnout. [learn more](GNS225_U5_T9#GNS225_U5_T9_h6)

question: What is the main goal of Community-Based Rehabilitation (CBR) programs?

options.A: To keep patients admitted in tertiary hospitals for long-term recovery
options.B: To provide acute surgical interventions for physical injuries
options.C: To connect patients with local resources and support for community living
options.D: To isolate individuals with disabilities from the general public

explanation: CBR programs bring rehabilitation and support services directly into the community to help individuals live active, integrated lives. [learn more](GNS225_U5_T9#GNS225_U5_T9_h7)

question: Which service helps a person with a physical disability return to productive work matching their current functional level?
explanation: Vocational rehabilitation programs assess remaining skills and train individuals for new jobs suited to their physical abilities. [learn more](GNS225_U5_T9#GNS225_U5_T9_h7)

question: How can a nurse best support self-advocacy in a patient with a physical disability?

options.A: By making all medical and lifestyle decisions on behalf of the patient
options.B: By encouraging the patient to voice their own healthcare choices and rights
options.C: By shielding the patient from interacting with unfamiliar community members
options.D: By filing formal legal complaints without consulting the patient first

explanation: Self-advocacy grows when nurses empower patients to speak up and make their own informed decisions about care and life. [learn more](GNS225_U5_T9#GNS225_U5_T9_h8)

question: What does social inclusion mean for a person living with a physical disability?

options.A: Depending entirely on family members for all daily social interactions
options.B: Living exclusively in specialized care facilities with other disabled peers
options.C: Having equal opportunities to work, learn, and participate in community life
options.D: Avoiding public spaces to prevent unwanted attention from strangers

explanation: Social inclusion ensures full participation in society, including employment, education, voting, and recreation. [learn more](GNS225_U5_T9#GNS225_U5_T9_h8)
